meta.title: Who really said "Art washes away from the soul the dust of everyday life"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Picasso. The line rewrites Berthold Auerbach’s 1864 sentence about music; the “art” version was pinned on Picasso in a 1964 Playboy piece.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Art washes away from the soul the dust of everyday life'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Picasso. It rewrites Berthold Auerbach’s 1864 line about music; the “art” variant first surfaced in a 1964 Playboy article.

answer.label: Not Pablo Picasso — adapted from Berthold Auerbach
answer.authorName: Berthold Auerbach (original); the “art” variant is anonymous
answer.authorDates: Auerbach: 1812–1882 · German novelist · the “art” rewording surfaced in 1964
answer.sourceLine: The line is a one-word rewrite of a sentence about music from Berthold Auerbach’s 1864 novel Auf der Höhe (“On the Heights”). Per Quote Investigator, the “art” version — swapping “music” for “art” — first appeared in a January 1964 Playboy feature titled “The Wisdom of Pablo Picasso,” with no source given. There is no evidence Picasso ever said or wrote it.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Music washes away from the soul the dust of everyday life.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the sentence to Berthold Auerbach’s 1864 novel Auf der Höhe, where the original German reads “…die Musik wäscht ihnen den Alltagsstaub von der Seele…”
The concise English form — “Music washes away from the soul the dust of everyday life” — descends from F. E. Bunnett’s 1867 translation and later quotation collections.
The art variant first appears in a January 1964 Playboy feature, “The Wisdom of Pablo Picasso,” with no source — QI judges the Picasso ascription “flawed” and likely spurious.
source.excerptNote: Auerbach’s original sentence is about music. The popular Picasso version simply replaces “music” with “art.”

source.rightsNote: The wording descends from Berthold Auerbach’s 1864 novel Auf der Höhe and its 1867 English translation by F. E. Bunnett — both long in the public domain. The only change in the Picasso-attributed version is the single word “music” → “art,” a trivial, anonymous 1964 substitution that carries no separate copyright.

author.name: Berthold Auerbach
author.heading: Whose words are these?
author.metaLine: 1812–1882 · German novelist & poet, author of Black Forest Village Stories
author.bio: Berthold Auerbach (1812–1882) was a German-Jewish writer best known for his Schwarzwälder Dorfgeschichten (“Black Forest Village Stories”). His 1864 novel Auf der Höhe (“On the Heights”) contains the sentence — about the cleansing power of music — that was later reworded into the famous line about art and misattributed to Picasso.

cite.sourceCitation: Berthold Auerbach, Auf der Höhe (1864); Eng. trans. as On the Heights by F. E. Bunnett (Leipzig: Tauchnitz, 1867). The “art” variant earliest documented in “The Wisdom of Pablo Picasso,” Playboy 11, no. 1 (January 1964): 95–97.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is a double misattribution: wrong author and wrong wording. The sentence is Auerbach’s, it was about music, and Picasso never said the “art” version.

items.why: The “art” wording first appears in a January 1964 Playboy feature, “The Wisdom of Pablo Picasso,” whose compiler is unidentified and gives no citation. Quote Investigator calls the ascription “flawed” and likely spurious.
Auerbach’s 1864 line reads “Music washes away from the soul the dust of everyday life.” The Picasso version merely replaces “music” with “art.”

misattribution.truthLine: The imagery is Berthold Auerbach’s, written about music in his 1864 novel Auf der Höhe; the “art” rewrite pinned on Picasso is an unsourced 1964 variant.

context.heading: Why it spread
lead: A tidy, uplifting sentence about art’s power, attached to the most famous artist of the 20th century, is almost designed to circulate. The 1964 Playboy compilation gave it a veneer of authority, and decades of poster shops, gallery walls, and social media did the rest — few readers ever traced it back to a German novelist writing about music a century earlier.
context.pull: The idea is real and old — it just belongs to Auerbach, and it was about music.
